sense: spend time with, keep company with

terms.gloss: spend time with, move among, associate with
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent; with cum and the ablative, or inter and the accusative
evidence: Sen. Ep. 7.8: cum hīs versāre, quī tē meliōrem factūrī sunt
Cic. Cat. 1.10: nōbīscum versārī jam diūtius nōn potes
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to move about in a place, i. e. to dwell, live, remain, stay, abide, be in a place or among certain persons”, with in, inter, apud or cum.

terms.gloss: be on close terms with, associate with (a person)
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, deponent, with the ablative; with familiāriter, of friendship
evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.3.1: multōs annōs ūtor valdē familiāriter
Cic. Att. 16.5.3: Luccejus, quī multum ūtitur Brūtō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to enjoy the friendship of any one; to be familiar or intimate with, to associate with a person”.

phrases.latin: Cum hīs versāre, quī tē meliōrem factūrī sunt. Illōs admitte, quōs tū potes facere meliōrēs. Mūtuō ista fīunt, et hominēs, dum docent, discunt.
phrases.english: Spend your time with those who will make you better; let in those whom you can make better. It works both ways: people learn while they teach.

phrases.latin: A. Trebōniō, quī in tuā prōvinciā magna negōtia et ampla et expedīta habet, multōs annōs ūtor valdē familiāriter
phrases.english: Aulus Trebonius, who has large and well-run business interests in your province, has been a close friend of mine for many years

sources: Lewis & Short: versor · Lewis & Short: utor
